title: THE BRIDE WHO BETRAYED HER BRIDEGROOM… AND THE KING WHO STILL CAME FOR HER
paragraphs: THE BRIDE WHO BETRAYED HER BRIDEGROOM… AND THE KING WHO STILL CAME FOR HER

Why does the Bible call the Church the Bride of Christ while warning so fiercely against sexual unfaithfulness? The answer exposes something deeper than sexual sin. It reveals the sacredness of covenant, the devastation of betrayal, and a Savior whose love is holy enough to confront our sin and merciful enough to redeem us.
What if the most terrifying thing about your secret sin isn't that Jesus might discover it… but that He already knows, and still calls you to come home?
Read that again.
He knows.

The conversation you deleted. The relationship you keep justifying. The private messages that would devastate your spouse. The images you promised yourself you would never look at again. The emotional attachment you insist is innocent, even though you know you are hiding it.
And perhaps your struggle isn't sexual at all.
Perhaps you've been faithful to your spouse but unfaithful to God.
You worship on Sunday, but your heart belongs to something else by Monday. You sing about surrender while secretly negotiating which parts of your life Jesus is allowed to touch.
And then you open your Bible and discover something extraordinary.
God does not merely call His people servants.
He calls them a bride.
Not because the Church has been perfectly faithful.
But because Jesus Christ is the Bridegroom who gave Himself to redeem and sanctify His people.
And suddenly, the Bible's warnings against sexual immorality begin to sound different.
They are not random restrictions imposed by a God who despises pleasure.

They come from the same God who created marriage, established covenant faithfulness, and chose the intimacy of a wedding to help us understand something astonishing about His relationship with His redeemed people.
But there is a question we must answer carefully.
If Christ loves the Church as His bride, why does Scripture speak so severely about adultery, fornication, lust, and spiritual unfaithfulness?
Why does the same Bible that celebrates the marriage supper of the Lamb warn that the sexually immoral will not inherit the kingdom of God apart from repentance and cleansing?
And why would God use the language of marriage to describe salvation in the first place?
The answer begins long before Bethlehem.
Long before the cross.
Long before the apostle Paul wrote to the Ephesians.
It begins with a covenant.
In the Old Testament, God repeatedly described His relationship with Israel using the language of marriage.
Through the prophet Hosea, the Lord declared:
“I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies.” — Hosea 2:19, KJV
The Hebrew word translated “I will betroth” is וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ (ve'erastikh), from the verb aras, meaning to betroth or pledge in marriage.
This is covenant language.
Not a casual romance.
Not a temporary emotional arrangement.
A solemn relationship of belonging, faithfulness, and commitment.
God was revealing His covenant love through an institution His people understood.
Marriage.
And when Israel turned toward idols, the prophets sometimes described that rebellion as adultery.
Not because every act of idolatry involved literal sexual activity.
But because worshiping false gods was a betrayal of covenant allegiance.
The people were giving their devotion to someone other than the One to whom they belonged.
That is why Hosea's story is so heartbreaking.
God commanded Hosea to enter a marriage that would become a prophetic picture of Israel's unfaithfulness and the Lord's persistent covenant love.
The story was not meant to romanticize betrayal, excuse abuse, or require a betrayed spouse to remain in danger.
It was a prophetic sign concerning God's relationship with His people.
And through it, God revealed a truth that should make every wandering heart tremble.
Sin is not merely the violation of a rule.
It is rebellion against the God who made us, loves us, and calls us to Himself.
But the story does not end with betrayal.
Through Hosea, God also promises restoration.
“I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.” — Hosea 14:4, KJV
Do you see the movement?
Unfaithfulness.
Exposure.
Judgment.
A call to return.
And the promise of mercy.
This is not permission to keep sinning.
It is an invitation to stop running.
Then Jesus enters the story.
And something remarkable happens.
When questioned about fasting, Jesus refers to Himself as the bridegroom.
“Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them?” — Matthew 9:15, KJV
That statement is easy to overlook.
But in the context of Israel's Scriptures, the imagery is profound.
The covenant relationship that the prophets described through marriage is now being brought into focus around Jesus Himself.
John the Baptist also identifies Jesus as the bridegroom.
“He that hath the bride is the bridegroom.” — John 3:29, KJV
John rejoices because the bridegroom has arrived.
The center of the story is not John.
It is Christ.
And that is where we must begin whenever we speak about the Church as the Bride of Christ.
The Bride is not the hero of the Gospel. The Bridegroom is.
The Church does not save herself by becoming beautiful enough, pure enough, or religious enough to deserve His love.
Jesus gives Himself for His people.
Listen to Paul's words:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
There is the heart of the mystery.
Christ loved the Church.
And gave Himself for her.
The Greek text reads:
Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς
Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian kai heauton paredōken hyper autēs.
A faithful translation is:
“Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
The verb ἠγάπησεν (ēgapēsen) means “loved.”
The verb παρέδωκεν (paredōken) means “handed over” or “gave up.”
Paul is not describing a Bridegroom who merely sends flowers, makes promises, or expresses affection.
He is describing Jesus surrendering Himself to death for the salvation of His people.
The Bridegroom goes to the cross.
Not because the Church is innocent.
But because sinners need redemption.
And this changes everything.
Because when Scripture calls the Church the Bride of Christ, it is not claiming that believers have a sexual relationship with Jesus.
The image is covenantal, corporate, and spiritual.
It communicates Christ's sacrificial love, His people's belonging to Him, their calling to faithfulness, and their future union with Him in everlasting glory.
Marriage is the earthly sign.
Christ and His Church are the greater reality toward which Paul directs our attention.
Paul continues:
“That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word.” — Ephesians 5:26, KJV
Notice what Jesus does.
He does not merely declare that sin does not matter.
He sanctifies.
He cleanses.
He transforms.
The Greek word ἁγιάσῃ (hagiasē), translated “sanctify,” means to make holy or set apart as holy.
This matters enormously.
Because the Gospel is not simply the announcement that Jesus accepts us while leaving us permanently enslaved to whatever destroys us.
It is the announcement that through His death and resurrection, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed by His grace.
Grace is not permission to remain in darkness.
Grace brings us into the light.
And now we begin to understand why the New Testament warns so seriously against sexual immorality.
Sex is not portrayed in Scripture as inherently dirty or shameful.
God created humanity male and female.
God established marriage.
Genesis 2:24 describes a man leaving his father and mother, cleaving to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
The Hebrew expression בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad) means “one flesh.”
This union involves more than physical intimacy alone. It describes the profound marital joining of two people in a shared life.
Jesus Himself affirms this creation pattern in Matthew 19:4–6.
Paul returns to the same passage in Ephesians 5.
“For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.” — Ephesians 5:31, KJV
Then comes the sentence that changes how we read the entire passage.
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.” — Ephesians 5:32, KJV
The Greek says:
τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν
To mystērion touto mega estin.
“This mystery is great.”
In Paul's writings, mystērion refers to a divine truth or purpose once hidden and now disclosed through God's revelation.
Paul is not saying that ordinary marriage and Christ's relationship with the Church are identical in every detail.
He is showing that marriage carries a significance greater than many people realize.
The covenant union of husband and wife points beyond itself to Christ and His Church.
And because marriage matters, faithfulness matters.
Because the body matters, sexual holiness matters.
Because love matters, betrayal matters.
But hear this carefully.
Sexual sin is not the only form of unfaithfulness, and sexual temptation is not the same as committing sexual sin.
The Bible does not teach that a person becomes spiritually worthless because they experience unwanted temptation.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
The issue is what we do with temptation.
Whether we resist it through God's grace or deliberately cultivate it.
Whether we flee from what leads us into sin or build a secret home for it in our hearts.
Paul writes:
The Greek word behind “fornication” is πορνεία (porneia), a broad term for sexual immorality.
Its precise application must be understood through biblical context rather than by forcing every modern debate into a single Greek word.
But Paul's central command is unmistakable.
Flee sexual immorality.
Not because the human body is worthless.
But because the body matters to God.
A few verses later, Paul reminds believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that they were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
This is a startling claim.
Your body is not spiritually irrelevant.
Your private choices are not disconnected from discipleship.
What you do when nobody is watching still matters before the God who sees you.
And perhaps that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to condemn the adultery we see in someone else's marriage while defending the lust we entertain in our own minds.
Easy to criticize someone else's public scandal while hiding our private compromises.
Easy to demand holiness from other believers while calling our own disobedience a complicated season.
But Jesus does not allow us to reduce faithfulness to appearances.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He teaches that deliberately looking at another person with lustful intent violates the heart of the commandment against adultery.
He reaches beneath outward behavior.
Into desire.
Into intention.
Into the secret places where sin often begins long before it becomes visible.
And suddenly, the question is no longer merely:
“Have I physically committed adultery?”
It becomes:
“Lord, what have I allowed to possess my heart?”
That question can hurt.
Especially when you already know the answer.
Maybe you are reading this while sitting beside someone who trusts you.
Maybe your marriage looks healthy in public, but there are conversations you would panic to see exposed.
Maybe you are single, exhausted by loneliness, and have started believing that sexual compromise is the price of being loved.
Maybe you have been betrayed and now wonder whether faithfulness means anything anymore.
Or maybe you are carrying the shame of something you did years ago, long after you confessed it, and you still struggle to believe that God can forgive you.
Please hear this.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend that betrayal is harmless.
But neither does it teach that sexual sin places a repentant sinner beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about serious sins, including sexual immorality, adultery, and idolatry.
Then he said something astonishing.
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
Such were some of you.
Were.
Not because their past had never happened.
Not because their choices had never wounded anyone.
Not because repentance erased every earthly consequence.
But because the saving work of Jesus Christ had changed their standing before God.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
This is what makes the Gospel so powerful.
It does not require us to rewrite our history before we can come to Christ.
It announces that Jesus can redeem people whose history they cannot rewrite.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8:1–11.

The passage is beloved, although responsible Bible study should acknowledge that John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is marked or discussed in many modern Bible editions.
Its familiar account nevertheless illustrates themes firmly established elsewhere in Scripture: mercy toward sinners and the call to leave sin behind.
Jesus does not join the crowd's eagerness to condemn the woman.
Yet He does not call adultery righteous.
The account ends with the command:
“Go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Mercy.
And holiness.
Not mercy instead of holiness.
Not holiness without mercy.
Both.
And that is precisely what we must remember when reading the warnings of the New Testament.
In Revelation 21:8, sexual immorality appears among the sins associated with final judgment.
In 1 Corinthians 6:9–10, Paul warns that those characterized by unrighteousness will not inherit the kingdom of God.
These warnings are real.
They must not be edited out of the Christian message simply because they make us uncomfortable.
But neither should they be twisted into the claim that anyone who has ever fallen sexually can never be saved.
The very next verse, 1 Corinthians 6:11, announces the cleansing and transformation of former sinners.
The New Testament's warnings confront unrepentant rebellion.
Its promises invite sinners to turn to Christ.
And that distinction matters.
Repentance is not the purchase price of forgiveness.
Jesus paid the price through His sacrifice.
Repentance is the turning from sin toward God that belongs to a living response of faith.

The Greek word commonly translated “repent” is μετανοέω (metanoeō), expressing a change of mind or turning of one's understanding and direction. In biblical proclamation, repentance involves a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in life.
It is not merely feeling guilty because you were caught.
It is not crying for one night and returning deliberately to the same deception the next morning.
It is not demanding that the person you betrayed immediately trust you again.
True repentance takes sin seriously.
It confesses rather than conceals.
It seeks to abandon what is wrong.
It accepts responsibility.
And where others have been harmed, it seeks appropriate repair without demanding that forgiveness remove consequences.
If you have betrayed your spouse, God's forgiveness does not entitle you to instant reconciliation or restored trust.
If you have been betrayed, the call to forgive does not require you to ignore danger, excuse ongoing abuse, or surrender wise boundaries.
God's holiness is never an excuse for cruelty.
And His mercy is never a license for continued deception.
Now consider something else.
In 2 Corinthians 11:2, Paul writes:
The Greek term παρθένον ἁγνήν (parthenon hagnēn) refers to a pure virgin.
Paul is using the imagery of betrothal to express the Church's exclusive devotion to Christ.
He is not saying that only physically virginal people can belong to Jesus.
That interpretation would contradict the Gospel's clear testimony that repentant sinners are cleansed and welcomed into God's people.
Paul is concerned that the Corinthians might be led away from sincere devotion to Christ through deception and false teaching.
The context makes that clear.
In the next verse, he warns about their minds being corrupted from sincere devotion to Christ, just as Eve was deceived by the serpent.
So the bridal imagery includes more than sexual conduct.
It concerns allegiance.
Truth.
Worship.
Faithfulness to Jesus.
And this exposes a danger that religious people can easily miss.
A person can avoid a public sexual scandal and still be spiritually unfaithful through idolatry, pride, greed, hypocrisy, or rejection of Christ's truth.
You can protect your reputation while neglecting your relationship with God.
You can appear morally respectable while trusting in your own righteousness rather than the Savior.
You can defend biblical marriage loudly while failing to love your own spouse sacrificially.
And you can preach purity without showing the compassion of Christ toward people struggling to repent.
Paul's words in Ephesians 5 do not give husbands permission to dominate their wives.
They command husbands to love with the self-giving pattern of Christ.
The passage calls believers toward holiness and sacrificial love, not manipulation or abuse.
The Bridegroom laid down His life.
He did not exploit His bride for selfish gratification.
And that brings us to the final scene.
Revelation 19.
Heaven is rejoicing.
The reign of God is being celebrated.
And John hears the announcement:
“Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready.” — Revelation 19:7, KJV
The Greek reads:
ὅτι ἦλθεν ὁ γάμος τοῦ ἀρνίου
Hoti ēlthen ho gamos tou arniou.
“For the marriage of the Lamb has come.”
The word γάμος (gamos) means marriage or wedding.
And ἀρνίον (arnion) means lamb.
The Bridegroom is the Lamb.
Do not rush past that.
The One who comes for His bride is the One who was slain.
The wedding celebration is inseparable from the sacrifice that made redemption possible.
And the next verse tells us that the bride was granted fine linen, clean and bright, representing the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8).
The Greek expression ἐδόθη αὐτῇ (edothē autē) means “it was given to her.”
That detail matters.
The bride is granted her clothing.
The passage also identifies the linen with the righteous deeds of God's holy people.
Grace and transformed living are not enemies.
God's grace produces a people whose lives bear witness to Him.
We are not saved because we have manufactured a flawless record of righteousness.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ, and we are created in Him for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10).
The wedding garment is not an excuse for self-righteousness.
It is a reason to glorify the God who redeems and transforms His people.
Then Revelation declares:
“Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb.” — Revelation 19:9, KJV
Imagine that.
The story that began with humanity's rebellion does not end with the triumph of sin.
It ends with the victory of the Lamb.
The redeemed gathered in joy.
The people of God dwelling with Him.
The promises fulfilled.
The shame of forgiven sinners no longer defining their identity.
The Bridegroom receiving the people He purchased with His blood.
And perhaps you are thinking:
“But what about me?”
“What about what I did?”
“What about the years I wasted?”
“What about the marriage I damaged?”
“What about the secret struggle I keep losing?”
“What if I have already gone too far?”
The answer is not found in pretending your sin was small.
The answer is found in the greatness of Jesus Christ.
John writes:
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a declaration that sin is harmless.
It is the announcement that Christ's saving work is sufficient for those who belong to Him.
You do not need to make peace with the darkness.
You can bring it into the light.
You do not need to pretend that your betrayal was love.
You can confess it for what it was.
You do not need to call your bondage freedom.
You can seek the help, accountability, and support necessary to walk in obedience.
And if you have been wounded by another person's unfaithfulness, remember this too.
Their betrayal does not determine your worth.
You are not responsible for another person's decision to sin against you.
God sees the wounds that other people minimize.
His compassion is not reserved only for the person who committed the wrong.
The Lord is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).
And healing does not always happen quickly.
Some wounds require time, wise pastoral care, trustworthy community, professional support, and patient rebuilding.
There is no shame in seeking help.
Now the question that began this article should finally make sense.
Why does the New Testament call the Church the Bride of Christ while warning against sexual unfaithfulness?
Because marriage is a sacred covenant that points beyond itself to the relationship between Christ and His Church.
Because sexual faithfulness matters within the marriage covenant God established.
Because spiritual unfaithfulness is a serious betrayal of our allegiance to God.
Because Jesus did not die merely to excuse sin, but to redeem sinners and make His people holy.
And because the final hope of the Church is not an eternity of religious performance.
It is everlasting fellowship with the risen Christ.
The Bridegroom who loved His people.
The Lamb who died for them.
The King who will bring His redeemed into the joy of His presence.
That is why the Church must not treat holiness as optional.
And that is why the Church must never preach holiness without the Gospel of grace.
We need both the warning and the invitation.
The warning tells us that sin is deadly serious.
The invitation tells us that Jesus is a mighty Savior.
And perhaps today, the most important response you can make is not to argue about someone else's failures.
It is to examine your own heart before God.
What have you been hiding?
What relationship needs to end?
What confession have you been avoiding?
What boundary needs to be restored?
What false god has been receiving the devotion that belongs to Christ?
What would genuine repentance look like in your life today?
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret conversation.
Not after another season of pretending.
Today.
Because the same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance also promises rest to those who come to Him (Matthew 11:28).
And no matter how stained your history may be, you do not have to make that history your permanent identity.
The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7).
That is not sentimental language.
That is Gospel truth.
So come to Him.
Confess what is true.
Trust what He has accomplished.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
And follow Him.
Not to earn His sacrifice.
But because His sacrifice is worthy of your whole life.

There is room here for honest testimonies too. Perhaps Christ has restored your life after a season you thought would destroy you. Your story, shared with wisdom and appropriate privacy, may remind someone else that repentance and redemption are real.
And please do not let this truth end with you.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be silently struggling with lust, pornography, infidelity, loneliness, guilt, or the devastation of betrayal.
Someone may have stopped attending church because they believe their past has disqualified them forever.
Someone may have heard plenty of condemnation but never understood the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Because spiritual growth rarely happens through one emotional moment alone.
We need the Word of God again tomorrow.
And the day after that.
We need truth when temptation returns.
We need encouragement when prayer feels difficult.
We need correction when pride begins to grow.
We need the Gospel when shame whispers that we are beyond forgiveness.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.

To continue proclaiming Jesus Christ, explaining Scripture faithfully, encouraging repentance, strengthening believers, and making biblical discipleship resources accessible to people who are hungry for truth.
And keeping resources accessible, developing new materials, and reaching more people requires ongoing support.
For those who choose to give regularly, that support can be offered to God as an act of generosity and worship.
But we must be clear about something important.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
These products can be meaningful reminders of biblical truth and useful tools for sharing encouragement with others. But the merchandise is never the heart of this ministry.
Jesus is.
The Word of God is.
The proclamation of repentance, forgiveness, and new life in Christ is.
We do not sell salvation.
We do not purchase God's favor.
We do not measure anyone's faith by their financial support.
We proclaim the Savior who freely gave Himself for sinners.
And we invite those who value this work to help make it available to others.
Because somewhere, a husband needs to repent before his secret destroys his family.
Somewhere, a wife is crying over a betrayal she never deserved.
Somewhere, a young believer is battling temptation and wondering whether purity is still possible.
Somewhere, a person who has spent years running from God is beginning to wonder whether the door of mercy is still open.
And somewhere, someone is about to read the words of Jesus and discover that their story does not have to end where their sin began.
That is why the Gospel must keep going.
Not because we are impressive.
But because Christ is worthy.
Not because our stories are spotless.
But because His grace is sufficient.
Not because we can save anyone.
But because Jesus Christ saves.
The Lamb who was slain is worthy.
The Bridegroom will be glorified.
And His redeemed people will rejoice in His presence.
Until then, may we live as people who belong to Him.
Faithful in public.
Faithful in private.
Quick to repent.
Ready to forgive.
Unwilling to excuse evil.
Unashamed of the Gospel.
And always remembering that the hope of the Bride is not her perfection apart from Christ.
It is the perfect Savior who loved her and gave Himself for her.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but it does not have to write the final sentence of the life you surrender to Jesus.
